home.title: Point at a leaf. Know what's wrong.
home.sub: LeafCheckup identifies {crops} leaf diseases from a single photo and tells you what to do about it. The AI runs on your phone, so it is free, private and works without internet.
home.conditionsSub: Each photo below is a real field image from the datasets the model was trained on, collected on farms in Rajasthan.

how.d: Fill the frame with a single leaf in daylight. Upload from the gallery or use the camera.

how.t: The model reads it on your device
how.d: An EfficientNet network checks the leaf twice, mirrored and unmirrored, and highlights the area that drove its answer. Your photo never leaves the phone.
You get the likely condition, how sure the model is, and field-tested steps to manage it. Save it, share it on WhatsApp or print a report.

home.evidenceSub: LeafCheckup comes out of research at BIT Mesra on diagnosing diseases of local Indian crops that large datasets ignore.
home.statAccuracy: accuracy on leaves the model never saw
home.statDownloads: downloads of the ridge gourd dataset on IEEE DataPort
home.pressLine: Featured in Punjab Kesari, Jaipur edition, 10 October 2025.
home.toolsSub: A diagnosis is the start. These tools help you decide, plan and record.
home.privacyTitle: Your photos stay on your phone
home.privacyBody: The model is downloaded once (about {mb} MB) and runs inside your browser. Nothing is uploaded unless you choose to share a report. After the first visit LeafCheckup works with no signal at all.
home.orgTitle: Free for everyone, open to builders
home.orgBody: No plans, no paywall. Farmers, extension workers and researchers use every tool for free, and developers can call the same model through a free API with fair-use limits.

faq.a: Yes, completely. There are no plans or paid features. Diagnosis runs on your own device, so it costs nothing to serve, and the developer API is free with fair-use limits.

faq.q: Which crops and diseases does it cover?
faq.a: {coverageDetail} If you photograph something else, LeafCheckup tells you it is not a supported leaf instead of guessing.

On a held-out set of leaves the model never saw during training it is right {acc}% of the time. It can still be wrong, especially on blurry photos or early symptoms, so treat it as a second opinion and confirm serious outbreaks with your KVK.

faq.q: How do I know the accuracy is genuine?
faq.a: The test leaves were set aside before training and never seen by the model. Many leaf datasets include several edited copies of each photo, and if copies of one leaf end up in both training and testing the score looks better than it is. LeafCheckup uses only the original photos, keeps every leaf in exactly one set, and removes near-identical and mislabelled photos. The model card on the Research page lists the full method, the confusion matrix and the known limitations.

faq.q: Is the research behind it published?
faq.a: Yes. LeafCheckup builds on a peer-reviewed paper in Springer's Communications in Computer and Information Science series, a review in Discover Artificial Intelligence, two public datasets on IEEE DataPort and Mendeley Data, and a registered Indian design for the field data-collection device. The Research page links to each one by its official DOI or registration number.

faq.q: Are my photos uploaded or stored?
faq.a: No. The AI runs inside your browser, so photos never leave your phone. Scan history is saved only on your device and you can delete it at any time. The site uses no advertising or tracking cookies.

faq.q: What if the result looks wrong?
faq.a: Retake the photo with one leaf filling the frame, in daylight and in focus, then compare the symptoms with the field guide for that disease. If the result stays unclear or the problem is spreading, show the plant to your Krishi Vigyan Kendra or an agronomist. LeafCheckup is a second opinion, not a replacement for one.

faq.q: Does it work on iPhone and Android?
faq.a: Yes. LeafCheckup runs in any modern browser, including Safari on iPhone and Chrome on Android, and on laptops. There is nothing to download from an app store.
Yes. After the first visit the app and model are stored on your phone. You can install LeafCheckup to your home screen from the browser menu.

Yes. Each new crop needs a labelled set of real field photos, so crops are added as those datasets are collected and checked. If you have one for a crop you grow, use the contact form on the About page.

Pranay Agarwal, a computer science graduate of BIT Mesra working on computer vision and AI for agriculture. LeafCheckup is based on his ridge gourd research. The About page has the full story and a contact form.

batch.title: Batch scan

batch.limit: Only the first 200 photos were added.

scout.title: Field survey
scout.sub: Estimate how much of a plot is affected. Walk a W or zig-zag path, scan one leaf from each plant you stop at, and LeafCheckup keeps the tally.
scout.incidenceNote: Share of scanned leaves with a disease. Scan at least 20 leaves for a useful estimate.
scout.none: No surveys yet. Start one when you are in the field.
scout.adviceLow: Low incidence. Remove affected leaves or plants and keep scouting weekly.
scout.adviceMid: Spreading. Act on the steps in the field guide this week and re-survey in 5–7 days.
scout.adviceHigh: High incidence. Act now and contact your KVK or agronomist.

risk.title: Weather risk outlook
risk.sub: Rule-of-thumb risk for the next 7 days, based on temperature, humidity and rain forecast for your location. It points to when to scout harder; it does not replace field checks.
risk.search: Or search a village or town
risk.methodBody: Whitefly and leaf miner build up fastest in warm, dry spells (about 25–35 °C, low rain). Phomopsis spreads in warm, humid, wet weather (about 24–32 °C, humidity above 80% or rain). Leafhoppers peak in hot weather. Scores combine these factors for each day. Weather data: Open-Meteo.
risk.error: Couldn't get the forecast. Check your connection and try again.
risk.denied: Location permission was refused. Search for your town instead.

calc.title: Spray mix calculator
calc.sub: Work out how much product goes in each tank. Always take the dose from the product label or your KVK.
calc.note: Typical knapsack tanks hold 15–16 litres. Spray volume depends on crop stage: ask your KVK. Wear gloves and a mask, and respect the pre-harvest interval on the label.

research.title: The research behind LeafCheckup
research.sub: Peer-reviewed papers, two open field datasets, a registered device design, and a model you can audit.
research.benchSub: The MIND-2025 paper reported 92.0% for DenseNet121 + XGBoost with augmentation applied before the train/test split, a limitation the paper itself flags. LeafCheckup re-evaluates on a split by source leaf, so no variant of a test leaf is seen in training.
research.dataQualityBody: Building the leaf-level split surfaced {conflicts} photos filed under two different labels and {dups} near-duplicate shots. Conflicting photos were excluded; duplicates were kept in the same split.

dev.title: LeafCheckup API
dev.sub: Send a leaf photo, get a diagnosis, calibrated probabilities and an out-of-distribution flag. JSON over HTTPS.
dev.authBody: Send your key in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. Keys are shown once; we store only a hash.
dev.limitsBody: Free for everyone. Images up to 8 MB (JPEG, PNG or WebP), 30 requests a minute and 5,000 a month per key. Responses include X-RateLimit-Remaining.
dev.playgroundBody: Paste a key and pick a photo to call the live API from your browser.
